questions.explanation_text: Benzene first reacts with concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ at $323-333\text{K}$ . This is nitration of benzene, and the product formed is nitrobenzene, marked as (A). $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}\overset{\text{Conc. HNO}_{3}/\text{Conc. H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2}\text{(A)}$ Nitrobenzene (A) is then reduced using $\text{Fe/HCl}$ . The nitro group, $-\text{NO}_{2}$ , changes into an amino group, $-\text{NH}_{2}$ . So the product is aniline, marked as (B). $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2}\overset{\text{Fe/HCl}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}\text{(B)}$ Aniline (B) reacts with $\text{NaNO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ at $273\text{K}$ . This reaction is called diazotization. It gives benzene diazonium chloride, marked as (C). $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}\overset{\text{NaNO}_{2}/\text{HCl},273\text{K}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}\text{(C)}$ Benzene diazonium chloride (C) is treated with ethanol, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ . Ethanol reduces benzene diazonium chloride to benzene. During this reaction, ethanol itself gets oxidised to acetaldehyde, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$ . $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}+\text{N}_{2}+\text{HCl}$ So, the organic compound D is acetaldehyde, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Benzene first reacts with concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ at $323-333\text{K}$ . This is nitration of benzene, and the product formed is nitrobenzene, marked as (A).

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}\overset{\text{Conc. HNO}_{3}/\text{Conc. H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2}\text{(A)}$

Nitrobenzene (A) is then reduced using $\text{Fe/HCl}$ . The nitro group, $-\text{NO}_{2}$ , changes into an amino group, $-\text{NH}_{2}$ . So the product is aniline, marked as (B).

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2}\overset{\text{Fe/HCl}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}\text{(B)}$

Aniline (B) reacts with $\text{NaNO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ at $273\text{K}$ . This reaction is called diazotization. It gives benzene diazonium chloride, marked as (C).

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}\overset{\text{NaNO}_{2}/\text{HCl},273\text{K}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}\text{(C)}$

Benzene diazonium chloride (C) is treated with ethanol, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ . Ethanol reduces benzene diazonium chloride to benzene. During this reaction, ethanol itself gets oxidised to acetaldehyde, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$ .

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}+\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}+\text{N}_{2}+\text{HCl}$

So, the organic compound D is acetaldehyde, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$ .

questions.question_text: Basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase is not decided by ________.
questions.question_html: Basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase is not decided by ________.
questions.explanation_text: Basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase is not decided by hyperconjugation effect . So, the correct option is: Option D: Hyperconjugation effect In aqueous solution, the basic strength of alkylamines mainly depends on: Inductive effect : Alkyl groups show $+I$ effect and increase electron density on nitrogen. Solvation effect : The conjugate acid formed after accepting $H^{+}$ is stabilised by water molecules. Steric hindrance : Bulky alkyl groups can reduce proper solvation and affect basicity. But hyperconjugation is not an important factor for deciding the basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase.
questions.explanation_html:
Basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase is not decided by hyperconjugation effect.

So, the correct option is:

Option D: Hyperconjugation effect

In aqueous solution, the basic strength of alkylamines mainly depends on:

  • Inductive effect: Alkyl groups show $+I$ effect and increase electron density on nitrogen.

  • Solvation effect: The conjugate acid formed after accepting $H^{+}$ is stabilised by water molecules.

  • Steric hindrance: Bulky alkyl groups can reduce proper solvation and affect basicity.

But hyperconjugation is not an important factor for deciding the basic strength of alkylamines in aqueous phase.

questions.question_html: Nitration of aniline in strong acidic medium gives significant amount of m-nitroaniline because

options.label: A
options.text: In electrophilic substitution reaction, amino group is meta directing
options.html: In electrophilic substitution reaction, amino group is meta directing

options.label: B
options.text: In strong acidic medium, aniline is present as anilinium ion.
options.html: In strong acidic medium, aniline is present as anilinium ion.

options.label: C
options.text: $-\text{NH}_{2}$ group always directs to meta position.
options.html: $-\text{NH}_{2}$ group always directs to meta position.

options.label: D
options.text: m-nitroaniline has higher molar mass than o & p nitroanilines.
options.html: m-nitroaniline has higher molar mass than o & p nitroanilines.

questions.explanation_text: The correct answer is Option B: In strong acidic medium, aniline is present as anilinium ion. Aniline has the group $-\text{NH}_{2}$ , which normally increases electron density on the benzene ring by resonance. So, under ordinary conditions, $-\text{NH}_{2}$ is ortho and para directing . But nitration is done using a strong acidic mixture, usually concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ . In this strongly acidic medium, the lone pair on nitrogen gets protonated: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}+\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ So aniline is converted into the anilinium ion , $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ . The group $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ is electron-withdrawing and meta directing . Because of this, nitration of aniline in strong acidic medium gives a significant amount of m-nitroaniline . So, the reason is: $-\text{NH}_{2}\overset{\text{strong acid}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ is meta directing. Hence, the correct option is B .
questions.explanation_html:
The correct answer is Option B: In strong acidic medium, aniline is present as anilinium ion.

Aniline has the group $-\text{NH}_{2}$ , which normally increases electron density on the benzene ring by resonance. So, under ordinary conditions, $-\text{NH}_{2}$ is ortho and para directing.

But nitration is done using a strong acidic mixture, usually concentrated $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ . In this strongly acidic medium, the lone pair on nitrogen gets protonated:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2}+\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$

So aniline is converted into the anilinium ion, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ .

The group $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ is electron-withdrawing and meta directing. Because of this, nitration of aniline in strong acidic medium gives a significant amount of m-nitroaniline.

So, the reason is:

$-\text{NH}_{2}\overset{\text{strong acid}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$

and $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ is meta directing.

Hence, the correct option is B.

questions.explanation_text: The only reagent that will “pick out” a primary aromatic amine (aniline) but not a secondary one (N-methylaniline) is the carbylamine test: • Carbylamine test (Option D: CHCl₃ + alcoholic KOH) – RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3 KOH → R–NC (isocyanide, foul smell) + 3 KCl + 3 H₂O – Only primary amines give the isocyanide; secondary amines (like N-methylaniline) do not react. Options A, B and C all react (or fail to react) with both aniline and N-methylaniline in essentially the same way, so they cannot be used to tell the two apart.
questions.explanation_html:
The only reagent that will “pick out” a primary aromatic amine (aniline) but not a secondary one (N-methylaniline) is the carbylamine test:

• Carbylamine test (Option D: CHCl₃ + alcoholic KOH)

– RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3 KOH → R–NC (isocyanide, foul smell) + 3 KCl + 3 H₂O

– Only primary amines give the isocyanide; secondary amines (like N-methylaniline) do not react.

Options A, B and C all react (or fail to react) with both aniline and N-methylaniline in essentially the same way, so they cannot be used to tell the two apart.

questions.question_html: Which of the following is least soluble in water at $298K$ ?
questions.explanation_text: Aniline $(C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2})$ is least soluble in water at $298K$ due to the presence of high molecular mass benzene ring present in ring. Lower aliphatic amines such as $CH_{3}NH_{2},(CH_{3})_{3}N$ and $(CH_{3})_{2}NH$ can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with water molecules and hence soluble in water. Solubility of amines decreases with increase in molar mass due to increase in the hydrophobic part which retard the formation of $H$ -bonds.

questions.question_text: During the fusion of organic compound with sodium metal, nitrogen present in the organic compound is converted into
questions.question_html: During the fusion of organic compound with sodium metal, nitrogen present in the organic compound is converted into
questions.explanation_text: When an organic compound containing nitrogen is fused with sodium metal—a procedure known as the sodium fusion test or Lassaigne's test—the nitrogen is transformed into a water-soluble salt. In this test, the conditions favor the formation of the cyanide ion. When the fused mass is dissolved in water, the nitrogen present is converted into sodium cyanide, which is written as: $NaCN$ This is the basis for subsequent confirmatory tests (such as the formation of Prussian blue when the solution is treated with ferrous sulfate). Thus, the correct answer is: Option C: $NaCN.$

questions.question_text: Which of the following will be the most stable diazonium salt $(RN_{2}^{+}X^{-})$ ?
questions.question_html: Which of the following will be the most stable diazonium salt $(RN_{2}^{+}X^{-})$ ?
questions.explanation_text: Understanding Diazonium Salts: Diazonium salts have the general formula $R-N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ , where $R$ is an organic group and $X$ is a counterion (like a halogen). The key to their stability is the nature of the $R$ group attached to the diazonium ion ( $N_{2}^{+}$ ). Stability Factors: Aromatic diazonium salts are generally more stable than aliphatic ones because the aromatic ring can help delocalize the positive charge. Now let’s look at the options: Option A: $CH_{3}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Methyl diazonium) - Aliphatic Option B: $CH_{3}CH_{2}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Ethyl diazonium) - Aliphatic Option C: $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Phenyl diazonium) - Aromatic Option D: $C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Benzyl diazonium) - Although it contains a benzene ring, it's considered aliphatic because the $N_{2}^{+}$ group is attached to the $-CH_{2}$ group, not directly to the benzene ring. Given this, the most stable diazonium salt is the one where the $N_{2}^{+}$ group is directly attached to a benzene ring, allowing for charge delocalization. So, the correct answer is: Option C: $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$

Stability Factors: Aromatic diazonium salts are generally more stable than aliphatic ones because the aromatic ring can help delocalize the positive charge.

Now let’s look at the options:

Option A: $CH_{3}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Methyl diazonium) - Aliphatic

Option B: $CH_{3}CH_{2}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Ethyl diazonium) - Aliphatic

Option C: $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Phenyl diazonium) - Aromatic

Option D: $C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$ (Benzyl diazonium) - Although it contains a benzene ring, it's considered aliphatic because the $N_{2}^{+}$ group is attached to the $-CH_{2}$ group, not directly to the benzene ring.

Given this, the most stable diazonium salt is the one where the $N_{2}^{+}$ group is directly attached to a benzene ring, allowing for charge delocalization.

So, the correct answer is:

Option C: $C_{6}H_{5}N_{2}^{+}X^{-}$
